title: Advanced Mixtures — Three-Component Alligation
tagline: Year 3 — Three-ingredient means, chained alligation, concentration changes and repeated replacement

introduction.overview: Year 2 handled two ingredients and the alligation cross. Year 3 mixes three or more ingredients, chains the cross when a mixture is itself used as an ingredient, tracks the concentration of a solution when water or pure acid is added, and handles replacement with different liquids. The weighted-average idea stays the same: the mean is the quantity-weighted average of the parts.
introduction.placementRelevance: Advanced mixture questions are commonly asked in the harder quantitative items of company aptitude rounds, usually with a chain of two operations.
introduction.realWorldContext: Blending grades of tea, preparing alloys and diluting chemical solutions in the laboratory follow exactly these rules.

learningObjectives: Compute the mean value of a three-component mixture
Track concentrations after adding water or pure solute
Solve repeated-replacement problems with different removals
Work backwards from a target mean

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Mean = Σ(quantity × value) ÷ Σ quantity. Alligation: cheaper : dearer = (dearer − mean) : (mean − cheaper). Water has value 0.

coreDefinitions: Weighted mean of several parts: Σ qᵢvᵢ / Σ qᵢ.
Chained alligation: first combine two ingredients into a composite whose value is their mean, then use the composite as a single ingredient.
Concentration: the fraction of the pure substance in a solution (alcohol 20% means 20 parts in 100).
Pure solute added: increases both the amount of solute and the total.
Replacement: removing x from a vessel of Q and replacing by another liquid multiplies the original by (1 − x/Q).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Every ingredient pulls the mean towards its own value in proportion to its quantity. With three ingredients, a clean way is to merge two into a temporary mixture, find its mean, and then treat the temporary mixture as one ingredient.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Write each ingredient as (quantity, value). Add the products and the quantities, divide, and compare with the target. For unknown quantities, merge two ingredients and apply the cross twice.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Three-component mean
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: Cost or concentration of the blend.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Chained alligation
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Mean of the first two, then cross with the third
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: Find the ratio of three items.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Adding water
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: New % = old amount of solute ÷ (total + water)

mainNarrative: For three ingredients, compute the weighted mean. 3 kg at ₹40, 5 kg at ₹60 and 2 kg at ₹50 cost 120 + 300 + 100 = ₹520 for 10 kg, a mean of ₹52 per kg.

To find the ratio of three items for a target mean, merge two of them. To make ₹32 from ₹20, ₹30 and ₹40 with the first two in equal parts, their composite is worth ₹25, and (40 − 32) : (32 − 25) = 8 : 7. Splitting the composite equally gives the ratio 4 : 4 : 7.

For concentration problems, the amount of pure solute is what is preserved when water is added. 40 L of 40% solution holds 16 L of solute. Adding 10 L of water gives 16/50 = 32%. Adding pure solute raises both the solute and the total, so write (6 + x)/(30 + x) = 0.4 to get x = 10.

Repeated replacement with different amounts multiplies the surviving fractions. From 60 L of milk, remove 6 L and replace with water (fraction left 54/60), then remove 12 L of the mixture (fraction left 48/60): milk = 60 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 43.2 L.
Selling a mixture at a profit uses the mixture cost: if 3 kg at ₹60 and 2 kg at ₹75 are mixed, the cost is ₹66 per kg and a 20% profit price is ₹79.20.

deepDiveAspects.title: Solving for an unknown quantity
deepDiveAspects.content: When one quantity is missing, set up the weighted-mean equation and solve the linear equation, or use the cross if only two parts are unknown.

deepDiveAspects.title: Water as a zero-value ingredient
deepDiveAspects.content: Water has concentration or price 0, so dilution problems are alligation problems with one end at zero.

solvedExamples.title: Three-ingredient mean
solvedExamples.question: 3 kg of tea at ₹40, 5 kg at ₹60 and 2 kg at ₹50 are mixed. Find the cost per kg of the mixture.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Each part is weighted by its quantity.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Averaging the three prices to get ₹50.

solvedExamples.title: Adding pure solute
solvedExamples.question: How much pure acid must be added to 30 litres of a 20% acid solution to make it 40%?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Solute plus x over total plus x.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Adding x to the solute only.

solvedExamples.title: Repeated replacement
solvedExamples.question: A vessel holds 60 L of milk. 6 L is removed and replaced with water; then 12 L of the mixture is removed and replaced with water. How much milk is left?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The second removal takes mixture, not pure milk.

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Solve simultaneous equations for three unknowns.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Merge two ingredients into a temporary mixture with its mean value, then apply one cross with the third.

commonMistakes.mistake: Changing the solute when adding water
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Keep solute fixed, change only the total.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: The mean must lie between the lowest and highest ingredient values; reject others.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Merge the two closest ingredients first.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Chained alligation is a two-step cross.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I find a three-ingredient mean?
Can I add acid to reach a target?
